keyVerseText: When I shall send Artemas unto thee, or Tychicus, be diligent to come unto me to Nicopolis: for I have determined there to winter.
rootMeaning: The name Ἀρτεμάς (Artemás) is etymologically contracted from a compound of Ἄρτεμις (Ártemis) and δῶρον (gift), meaning 'gift of Artemis.' Artemis, originally a Grecian goddess associated with the moon and hunting, was known as a prompt or swift deity. This root meaning adds a layer of cultural and linguistic depth beyond the simple English transliteration, suggesting that the name carries a notion of a divine or precious gift, possibly reflecting the early Christian practice of adopting and transforming pagan names into new spiritual identities.
usageInScripture: The word Ἀρτεμάς occurs only once in Scripture, specifically in Titus 3:12, where it is translated simply as 'Artemas.' This singular occurrence indicates that the name is used as a proper noun, referring to a Christian individual rather than a common noun or concept. The consistent translation as a personal name highlights the historical reality of early Christians bearing names with pagan origins, yet serving God's purposes within the New Testament narrative.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding Ἀρτεμάς as 'gift of Artemis' reminds believers that God can redeem and repurpose even names or cultural elements rooted in paganism for His sovereign plan. The presence of such a name in the New Testament underscores the inclusivity of the gospel and the transformative power of Christ to sanctify all aspects of life, including identity. It also reflects the reality that early Christians often navigated a world filled with diverse religious influences, yet remained faithful witnesses. This name, borne by a Christian servant, serves as a testament to God's grace extending into every cultural context, affirming that our identities are ultimately shaped by Him rather than by worldly origins.
keyVerseReflection: In Titus 3:12, Paul writes, 'When I shall send Artemas unto thee, or Tychicus, be diligent to come unto me to Nicopolis: for I have determined there to winter.' The mention of Artemas here highlights him as a trusted Christian companion sent on a mission, emphasizing the personal and relational nature of ministry. The name Artemas, carrying the meaning 'gift of Artemis,' enriches the verse by reminding us that God can use individuals from varied backgrounds as valuable gifts to advance the gospel. This encourages believers to recognize and embrace their God-given roles within His redemptive plan.
